utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you call the case, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Mr. Mathias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, our case manager, Andres Vatter, and we are accompanied today by our intern, Mr. Kyle Wood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Alexis Demirdjian, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [Interpretation] This morning we have a witness on the agenda. Mr. Mundis wasn't hearing. I was saying that on the agenda we have the hearing of a witness. Is this witness at the disposal of the Chamber, Mr. Mundis? Is he available?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: He is indeed available, Mr. President, and I believe he's waiting in the witness waiting room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, will you be kind enough to go and fetch this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Let me check that you are hearing the translation of my words. If that is so, please tell me so, that you are hearing me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As it's okay, we can continue. You have been called as a witness for the Prosecution. You will therefore take the solemn declaration. Before you do that, I need to know your identity. So will you please tell me your first and last name, date and place of birth, and nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Mats Torping. I am born 16th of April, 1943 in Stockholm, Sweden, and I am a Swedish citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At present I am retired, but I still am an officer, lieutenant colonel, in the Swedish Army Reserve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993 in Bosnia and Herzegovina, what were your positions in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was monitor of the ECMM, December 1992 to March 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you previously testified in a national court of law or in an international court on the events that occurred in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or is this the first time for you to testify in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I haven't testified yet. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be kind enough to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to representatives of the Prosecution, I should like to provide some information regarding the proceedings here. As this is the first time that you are testifying in an international court of law, it is my duty to provide some explanations regarding the way we will proceed today during your testimony. During the first stage, you will be answering questions that will be put to you by representatives of the Prosecution, who are seated to your right, and who will have questions for you within the framework of the procedure defined by the Rules of Procedure, that is known as the examination-in-chief. This examination will last a certain amount of time, and upon the completion of the questions of the Prosecution, whom I'm sure you have met before this morning, the Defence attorneys, who are seated on your left and in two rows and who represent the two accused, who are also in the courtroom, will have questions for you as part of the cross-examination. This cross-examination gives the Defence counsel the opportunity to verify the statements of the witness or to clarify certain elements of the background which may throw additional light and support to the position of the Defence, and you will see that their questions will be quite different from those put to you by the Prosecution. Upon the completion of this stage, the Prosecution may have some additional questions for you. The three Judges, seated directly in front of you, may ask you questions at any stage of the proceedings, but the Judges prefer to wait until the end of the three previous stages - that is, the examination-in-chief, cross-examination, re-examination - to put their questions to you, because frequently the questions that the Judges may have in mind may be put by either of the parties, so there's no point for the Judges to intervene, so it is better to allow the parties to go first. And if the Judges need further clarification or certain areas that are unclear, they will have questions for you. As you know -- no, you don't know, but I wish to let you know that the procedure is basically an oral procedure. Sometimes it is complemented with written documents which are produced during the testimony of a witness. But as the procedure is mainly oral, what is crucial are the answers given by the witness to questions put to him. Hence the importance of the answers that you are going to give. Try and be precise and concise at the same time. If you don't remember something, as the events took place more than ten days ago [as interpreted] and one's memory may fail one, please let us know f a question appears to be complicated or confused, then ask the person asking you the question to rephrase it. It is very important for you to understand the meaning of a question. So if you don't understand it, ask the party to reformulate it in an understandable fashion. I have two other points to draw your attention to: You have made the solemn declaration to tell the whole truth, which excludes the possibility of false testimony, because as you know, false testimony is an offence which can be sanctioned; there is another provision that certainly won't apply to you but which I need to refer to, is that should a witness be asked a question that could incriminate him, he may refuse to answer it. Should that occur, as envisaged in a number of countries, common-law and civil-law countries, the witness may refuse to answer. In that very particular case, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer; however, at the same time the Chamber guarantees the witness a type of immunity. So in very general terms, that would be the way in which these proceedings will evolve. I wanted to tell you in advance so that your hearing and testimony may take place under the best possible conditions. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mr. Mundis, as you are alone, I assume you will start with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Torping.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told the Chamber that you are a retired lieutenant colonel in the Swedish Army. Can you please tell us from the time you joined the Swedish Army until the time of your retirement the various positions and assignments that you held in the Swedish Army, with particular emphasis on international deployments.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Okay. I started my military service as a conscript, as all male Swedes did at that time, 1962. I was promoted second lieutenant colonel -- second lieutenant after officer's training in 1965. In the beginning I served with my regiment, which is an armoured regiment, training soldiers and conscripts officers. After that, I have been instructor in war academy, military staff college for becoming officers, cadets, as well as young officers. I've also been corps commander for armoured corps of two years. My military international experience started when I passed the Nordic training for military observers in Finland, 1984, and then I left for the Middle East, where I -- in Israel in the organisation UNTSO, United Nations Troop Supervision Organisation. Was military observer for one year in the area of Golan and south of Lebanon. 1989 to 1991, one and a half years, I was chief of the observer group of UNTSO on Golan, stationed in Damascus, also with some tasks in south of Lebanon and Beirut. 1992, I was selected being a monitor of the European Commission Monitor Mission, one of the Swedes there, and I had some additional training in the Swedish UN centre before going to December to Zagreb, and then I stayed for three months with ECMM as a monitor, all time in Bosnia except one week in Split. My next international commitment was when I was chief of the observer group in UNTSO, both sides of Golan area for one year, 1995 to 1996. When I was chief of this observer group, I had a lot of liaison duties with the other UN forces, UNDOF, as well as both Israeli and Syrian as well as Lebanese military authorities. My last international task was to be a chief instructor of an observer course in Germany with Bundeswehr 1997, when I was for one and a half months in Hammelburg, the German UN centre, training, becoming military observers from different countries of Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us about being an ECMM monitor in late 1992, early 1993. Other than that experience, did you have any deployments in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. After returning home spring 1993 - I really forgot it - I became a member of the becoming 1st Nordic Battalion, the training of the 1st Nordic Battalion belonging to UNPROFOR in spring and summer 1993, and I was the senior liaison officer to this Nordic Battalion of UNPROFOR in September 1993 to April 1994. That battalion had its main area of responsibility in the Tuzla region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Torping. I'd like to focus your attention now on the ECMM deployment. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what type of specific briefings regarding the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina you received prior to that deployment.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: There was some strange in here -- okay. Before going to former Yugoslavia, I, like other becoming monitors - we were two at that time, going together - we received a lot of information briefings concerning the situation in former Yugoslavia in the UN training centre in Sweden in Almnas. We didn't know at that time to which part of former Yugoslavia we should go, if it was Croatia, Bosnia, or Serbia, or whatever; so we had a general briefing. But we were informed of the military situation as long it was known, the political situation, the social situation, also the ethnical situation. So I think I had a rather good, general impression of the situation as such. When we came to the HQ of ECMM in Zagreb, we got additional and the latest news concerning the situation during -- I think it was two, two and a half day of different briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go following the briefing at the headquarters of ECMM in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: After these approximately three days in Zagreb, I left for Split, because I was supposed to be stationed with the Regional Centre Split. And in Split I stayed for an additional three, four days, getting more detailed information, briefings concerning the situation in the area of responsibility for Regional Centre Split and Regional Centre Split area of responsibility was that part of Bosnia controlled by the Bosnian government and -- yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I also got briefings concerning the SOPs, standard operating procedures, of ECMM and the staff work of Regional Centre Split. So I was acquainted with the terrain as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, what date did you arrive in Split?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It was just before Christmas eve, if it was 22nd or 23rd -- 22nd, I think, December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in Split?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I arrived in Zenica, which was the next station, 27th of December, so it should be four or five days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time you arrived in Zenica, was there an ECMM regional centre established in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No. The only presence of ECMM in Central Bosnia in the Zenica region, that was Team Zenica, consisting of two monitors, one of them team leader. And this time it was Jim Guilford, a Canadian officer. And I replaced another monitor who was to go home. Additionally, there was another ECMM driver, a non-commissioned driver from the French forces. And then we had some local interpreters, but that was all of ECMM presence in Zenica region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So I take it, then, from your answer that the regional centre Zenica was established some time after your arrival and you reported to RC Split.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the Central Bosnia region on this deployment?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I spent my three months with ECMM in Central Bosnia, but it was in two parts. The first part was from 27th of December to 1st of February, when I left going back to Split for the leave. And at that time I didn't know if I should return to Team Zenica or some other activities in Zenica. After two weeks, one week leave plus some staff work in Regional Centre Split, I was ordered to go back to Zenica, and I returned to Zenica, I think, the 17th of February.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, which year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following this return on 17 February 1993, how long did you remain in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I remained in Zenica to the end of my tour with ECMM, and that was -- I think I left Zenica 28th, maybe 27th of March, 1993, going via Split back to Zagreb and then home to Sweden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the entire time period that you were in Zenica - again, I understand you were out of Zenica for two weeks in February - but during the period from late December 1992 until the end of March 1993, what was the area of responsibility that your team monitored?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: The area of responsibility for our team in the beginning and then for the UN commission -- sorry, not UN commission but becoming regional centre of Zenica was the Central Bosnia controlled by Bosnian government. That means the region, Zenica, east to Kladanj, Visoko, south, Kiseljak, Konjic, direction west, including Gornji Vakuf; direction north, Tesanj, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and as far possible to go to the front line to the Bosnian Serbs, north of Travnik. Travnik also, and Grude belonged to our area of responsibility, but north of that area. The Bosnian Serbs had control and we couldn't go into that direction because then we were fired at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, you've mentioned the Bosnian Serbs. Can you tell us what other parties were active in the area that you monitored during the time period you were there.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Well, in the area of our responsibility, we have the HVO, the military organisation of the Bosnian Croats; we had their HQ in Vitez. Of course, as a monitor, we didn't only monitor the military situation but also the political situation, the social, economical, even ethnical situation, so we had also interest in having contacts with the political organisations. I am referring in that case, concerning the Bosnian Croats, to HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the Croat military organisation and political parties, what other groups were in the area that you monitored?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Except HVO, from the military point of view, it was the BiH army. Also there were some small organisations on the Croat -- Bosnian Croat side, HOS, very limited but existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, which unit or units of the BiH army were in the area you monitored?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Concerning BiH army, the unit of control of that area was 3rd Corps BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us a little bit about the first, say, week to two weeks that you were in Bosnia. What efforts were undertaken to introduce you to the key leaders in the area that you monitored?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I can say that my first impression was that situation inside the area was rather calm. We, the team, had a large area and we were just two persons, two monitors, one vehicle. So it was a huge area to know. I was by the team leader introduced to, had meetings with 2nd Corps, of course, with HVO, with the mayor of -- sorry, 2nd Corps -- I meant 3rd Corps, of course -- with the mayor of Zenica. Also I met the Serb Orthodox priest in Zenica, as well as Roman Catholic priest in Zenica, and also we had a meeting with the imam or the representative of the imam in Zenica. Also we had meetings with the local Red Cross of Zenica, and I met the chief of police in Zenica, who provided a national or a civilian national ID card to us, which we never used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us you met with -- or you had meetings with the 3rd Corps. Do you recall whom in the 3rd Corps you met with during the first, say, two weeks of your deployment to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I think it was the second or maybe the third day of -- after my arrival in Zenica. We had a meeting with Selmo Cikotic, and he was the liaison officer of 3rd Corps. Also he spoke very good English compared to many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the liaison officer, with whom did you meet?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Other than the commanders, local commanders and commanders different levels. What I can remember now, it was just another liaison officer -- I can't remember his name exactly, Husic or something like that. And he didn't speak too good English, but Selmo, he was definitely much, much better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that you met with local commanders and commanders at different levels. How senior were the leaders that you met with in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: After some days - I don't remember exactly the date, if it was the 6th or something like that January - a meeting was organised by Selmo with commander 3rd Corps, Mr. -- at that time Mr. Hadzihasanovic, and it was, so to say, a social meeting in that way that he should know us or should know me and I should know him, and we discussed in general the situation or so. If his deputy, Mr. Merdan, was present at that time, I can't remember. Also I would say I had a meeting with the local HVO commander in Zenica. He was said to be a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall that individual's name?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I have it in my notes. And if I hear a name, I should remember it. But sorry, I can't remember it myself now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, throughout the period that you were in Central Bosnia on this ECMM deployment, approximately how many times did you have any type of meeting or direct exchange with Mr. Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Six or seven times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And throughout the period that you were in Central Bosnia on this ECMM deployment, approximately how many times did you have any type of meeting or exchange with Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was not too often, but later on, when the joint commission was formed, he became a member of this joint commission, and I met him, I would say, every day because we worked rather tight together in this joint commission, he and the Bosnian -- other Bosnian officers, as well as the HVO officers, Mr. Nakic, me myself and my other monitor. So in the later part every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll ask you some questions about the joint commission in just a few moments. Before I do that, however, I'd like to ask you a little bit about overall responsibilities and duties that you had, particularly in the time period until you went on leave in early February, that is, from your arrival through the month of January 1993. What were your primary duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I as a member of this team - we were two - had a responsibility to supervise, to monitor the situation - as I said earlier, militarily, politically, socially, from ethnical point of view and also from a humanitarian point of view. We had a lot of cooperation with UNHCR as well as some cooperation with ICRC. We reported to Regional Centre Split every evening, and we felt our responsibility was to know the area, the situation, and when possible try to help in solving problems between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, you've told us that you met with a number of political leaders as well as military leaders. Do you recall some of the political leaders that you met in the area that you monitored?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I had a meeting with the mayor, Besim Spahic I think was his name. We discussed the situation, and also he, like other local leaders, passed to us the needs of the society, for the population, concerning food, medical care, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I could ask a clarification question. You mentioned a meeting with the mayor, whose name you think was Besim Spahic.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember what town or village or city he was the mayor of?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: He was the mayor of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the mayor of Zenica, did you meet with any other mayors or political leaders?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. When we were in different areas, we normally met the military local commanders, as well as the political leaders. And, for example, we were in Zavidovici in the at the. We met the brigade commander of BiH army at that area as well as the local leader, which -- whose name I have forgotten. Another important area was, of course, the Bosnian Croat-dominated Vitez area, and we had some meetings with the mayor of Vitez, who was also, he said, the local commander of the Territorial Defence of Vitez. He was a person -- I forgot the name, but I remember he spoke rather good German, and that meant that we could communicate in German directly. Normally we used our interpreters. We had four interpreters, one on duty each day. And more or less all communication with others than this mayor was in, what I say, Serbo-Croat language, which I can't understand, so -- as well as Jim Guilford and the other monitors didn't understand it either. So we had to rely on our own local interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, do you recall any of the subject matters of the discussion that you had with the mayor of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that rather clear. A meeting was requested and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. we went for Vitez from Zenica, but when we came to Vitez to meet him, he wasn't there. He had left for Travnik for some reason. We left also for Travnik where we met him in the local HVO place in Travnik, and he said he was very concerned because there were, according to his opinion, a lot of Mujahedin fighters. He said -- he mentioned a figure of approximately 2.000. We had heard earlier - but I don't recall exactly from whom - that there could be some Mujahedin fighters, but he was the one pointing out more strongly these accusations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, if I could briefly interrupt. Do you recall approximately when this meeting was with the mayor of Vitez, the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Sometime mid-January, but I don't remember exact date if I don't look in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, that would be 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether or not he gave you some additional information about the location of these foreign fighters that he told you about?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yeah. He said not exactly but could be in Travnik -- could be east of Zenica, it could be north of Vitez. And after ending the meeting with him, we went around in Travnik trying to find -- to see ourselves if there were any trace and to find some military HQ where we could check the situation, and we found the building where soldiers went in, so we followed some soldiers into this building in the centre of Travnik and went up one or two floors. We met some soldier. He asked what we were doing, and -- via the interpreter -- and then came a person, and he presented him as a commander or instruction officer, and we passed a question to him and looked around ourselves if there were some Mujahedin fighters or foreign fighters. He stated that there were no foreign fighters; it was just Bosnians in the brigade, and he stated it was part of the 7th Muslimanski Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the individual you spoke to?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No. And he didn't want to present himself and I got the general opinion he was not too happy seeing us in that building, but he didn't force us out. But he didn't want to have any long discussion, but he stated no foreign fighters were hidden in his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, for purposes of identification, he identified himself as the commander or instruction officer?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Not exactly, but he was dressed like most other BiH soldiers. What I can remember, he had no badge, because we looked at the badges here. It was one of the few ways to try to identify different units, but he had no one. But there were a lot of soldiers having no badges and so on, and they had no ranks at all during this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record, when the witness indicated "here," he was pointing to his left shoulder -- upper shoulder on his jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Torping, in addition to this meeting or encounter, if you will, in this building in Travnik, what steps did you take, if any, to verify or to ascertain additional information concerning these foreign fighters with other people in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Later when we met corps commander 3rd Corps, I brought up this matter, and the answer was, "There are no foreign fighters with 3rd Corps. It's only local Bosnian soldiers." And this statement I got in other situations from other persons also; among others, from Mr. Merdan, but others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many times you raised this issue with leaders of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It's difficult to say, but I would say maybe five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say "later when we met corps commander 3rd Corps I brought up this matter," whom were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I was referring to the commander 3rd Corps, Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me now turn to the joint commission that you mentioned earlier. What was the formal name of the joint commission that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: The first name, I think it was 28th of January, we were ordered by the head Regional Centre Split to form a Joint Commission for Cease-fire, and that was cease-fire between BiH army and HVO because of the fighting in the area mainly around or north and west of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more information about how this joint commission in Busovaca was established.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: In the beginning, it was the Team Zenica getting this task, and we organised ourselves in the neighbourhood of the Dutch-Belge transport battalion location in Busovaca, and we got members from both BiH army and HVO in Central Bosnia to participate in this joint commission. And the idea was that we should together try to, when happens -- happenings came, solve the problem locally and calm down the feelings and -- the hostile feelings between, for example, different villages, Croat village, Muslim villages shooting to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that there were members from both BiH army and HVO in Central Bosnia participating in this joint commission. Do you recall the names of the individuals from those two parties who regularly attended these commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: From 3rd Corps, Mr. Merdan, the deputy, was participating; and from HVO Central Bosnia, it was Mr. Nakic. He was also the deputy or Chief of Staff HVO Central Bosnia. So it was to our opinion high-ranking members of the two parties, which we considered very positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was this joint commission up and running before you went on your leave in early February 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I remember, it was organised 28th and some day -- and we had, so to say, regular meetings each day -- some day two, days after - I don't remember exactly - there were some information. It was a very tense situation in some village or between some villages, I think, in north-west of Busovaca, and we left for this area. We were supported because of it was rather dangerous going around among shooting people -- we were supported by the Danish HQ company of UNPROFOR in Kiseljak with an armoured personnel carrier, an APC, and we left, Mr. Merdan, Mr. Nakic, me myself and another monitor, to go directly to this village, and the first one we came to was a Bosnian Croat village, and we tried to find out what was going on. We couldn't find any actual fighting. It was mainly rumours or people were very afraid of the other side should attack them and so on. It was when these Bosnian Croat members of the village - and they were at the same time members, some males, of the HVO, the local HVO militia - when they found out it was a BiH army member, they were very critical, hostile, and they didn't want us to go. Mr. Nakic, from their own side, HVO, he had a lot of work trying to convince them that it was a good solution and we tried to solve the problems. And we came out without any problem. But definitely, the two sides - in this case the Bosnian Croat side - were very, very hostile too, afraid of the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, if I could again interrupt you. Let me take you to the time after you returned from your leave. Do you recall the approximate date you returned to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I returned the 17th of February, and at that situation I was supposed to be a staff member of the becoming RC Zenica, so I started working with some staff matters, but also I took part in the activities in the field by the joint commission, because we were short of manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us how your responsibilities changed with respect to the joint commission after your return from leave.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. If I go back slightly. The first chairman of the joint commission was an English monitor, Jeremy Fleming. After a while, he was replaced when he went for leave, I think, by a Dutch monitor, Kees van der Pluijm. But the 24th of February we got the message that I was from 25th of February to become the new chairman of the Joint Commission of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Busovaca, which was the name at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, what exactly did the joint commission do in this period of late February and into March 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: In general, we had the same tasks as earlier. We met every morning in Busovaca in the beginning, then we moved to Vitez afterwards, to inform each other of the situation and where there were hot spots and where it was necessary to be present, take action, and so on. So we were, so to say, an organisation supposed to work ad hoc when needs came up, which it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How were the parties to these joint commissions, how did they travel to the joint commission meetings?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: At this time, the joint commission consisted of the ECMM parts, normally two monitors; and from BiH army, Mr. Merdan, plus two other 3rd Corps Staff officers. From HVO, Mr. Nakic remained, and he had also two staff officers from HVO HQ in Vitez. So we were totally approximately eight, plus the driver and so on. And concerning the transports, the situation was that we had our place, our small HQ, in Busovaca next to this Dutch-Belge transport battalion. This was inside HVO-controlled area. And because of that I had to arrange - either myself driving or another monitor - to collect the BiH army representatives, Mr. Merdan and two others, each morning and transport them to Busovaca, and the same when the work ended in the evening; we transported them back to Zenica. And normally the contact point was next to 3rd Corps HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, again, for clarification, you would pick them up --

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- next to the 3rd Corps HQ and return them to that same location.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned two BiH staff members who were members of the commission and accompanied Mr. Merdan. Do you remember the names of those two individuals?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: One was Mr. Veser [phoen] and the other Mr. Sefer -- Sifir -- Sefat [phoen], I think. And he was replaced in the end of my tour by another one. I have forgotten the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these two individuals that accompanied Mr. Merdan junior to Mr. Merdan or senior to Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: They were junior concerning duty, because he was the deputy of the corps. He was the head of the BiH army representatives in this joint commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us that the pick-up point was next to the 3rd Corps headquarters. Can you please tell us where the 3rd Corps headquarters was located.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps HQ was located next to the big steel factory in Zenica in the northern part of the city in a building which I believe belonged to or had belonged to the steel factory earlier. It was a building for, if I say so, administrative matters normally, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you ever inside the 3rd Corps headquarters building?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Each time we had a meeting, me and my teammate - we were always two - we had it inside. When we met Mr. Hadzihasanovic, we met inside the building, normally I think all times in the room where Mr. Hadzihasanovic worked normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us that on approximately six occasions you met with Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Do you recall some of the subject matters that were discussed with him at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. I think after the first introduction, if I call it like that, one serious matter we had a meeting - it could have been mid-January - was that HVO, chief of HVO, Tihomir Blaskic, had threatened to shell Zenica if 3rd Corps reinforced their forces in the area north Busovaca-Vitez. And he threatened, so to say, to shell the town if this reinforcement continued and was not stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any other subjects that you discussed with Mr. Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Another subject was -- and that was, as a matter of fact, just after, when we, the team, was contacted by the local HVO HDZ in Zenica, and they told us that four -- sorry, 14 Bosnian Croats in three villages east of Busovaca had been captured and after that killed by Muslim forces. And the corpses had been brought to the hospital of Zenica and some relatives, refugees, had been brought by bus to Zenica, where they were accommodated by relatives and other Bosnian Croat families. And now the HDZ HVO wanted us to help in clarifying the situation and most important, to organise and transport these refugees to Vitez, which they thought were more secure for these people. And this matter we discussed with Mr. Hadzihasanovic in his HQ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, of these approximately six meetings that you had with Mr. Hadzihasanovic, were all of these professional meetings or were any of them or could any of them be characterised as social events?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, at least one -- or I would say one was a typical social event because of -- I think it was the 6th of March, we, the joint commission -- or the ECMM part of the joint commission, as well, of course, as the BiH army part of the joint commission, we were invited to a dinner hosted by corps commander 3rd Corps in a dining hall next to the HQ 3rd Corps. And we were offered good food, something to drink, and it was a nice, friendly atmosphere. Later in the evening, we were invited by the corps commander to visit the underground part of 3rd Corps building where corps commander showed us what we -- what I should call was command central, with capacity for staff work and so on, as well as communication and so on. That was what I understand the command post for commander 3rd Corps when he, so to say, commanded and controlled his forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, let me again ask you some questions by way of clarification. You've told us this was on the 6th of March. Again, what year was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us approximately how many ECMM personnel were present at this dinner and then accompanied you to this command post.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I think we were -- I think we were three. It was me myself; it was monitor Canadian Brad Koski; and I think Danish monitor Erik Friis-Pedersen was with too. I'm not sure, but I think he was with. Of course, we had our interpreters with too, because we have to use them for communication, even concerning the social part of the life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about what the purpose of this dinner was, and, if you know, why you were then taken to this command post following the dinner.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: My impression was that 3rd Corps wanted to build up and keep a good atmosphere, relation with us as ECMM members. If it was because commander 3rd Corps believed that this joint commission had a positive effect on the situation or not, I do not know, but I think it was to create a good, positive working climate and maybe an understanding from our point to the situation of the Bosnian side 3rd Corps, and also the situation of the area of Zenica, controlled by Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Also, maybe this -- because you asked about the visit underground -- maybe it was a way to show that the corps commander had some resources for his job to command and control the forces; compared to in the beginning the first meetings when we were briefed of the situation I got the opinion that the corps commander, his point of view was that the resources totally were very limited for 3rd Corps and he had maybe problems in totally controlling all parts all the. I don't know, because I got the impression 3rd Corps had very limited resources for communication in the beginning. Maybe now they had better, in early March, better resources as such. And we saw a lot of radios, not familiar to me, because it was former Yugoslavian radios or Russian type, I do not know. But it was a lot of radios. And as a matter of fact, I saw a fax too at that situation. We saw a lot of maps, of course covered Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. so we couldn't see the actual situation. But it gave me an impression of a professional place for command and control of a commander of a corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how large this room was?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: My opinion is, but I'm not sure exactly, but let's say 5 or 7 metres square, 10 or 15, something like that. Let's say 6 square 12, something like that. It was a rather large room, and it was said to be proof for shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "it was said to be proof for shelling," who told you that and what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly who told me. Maybe it was Mr. Merdan, because often he and I, we walked together talking, okay, through the interpreter. Concerning shelling, I presume he meant -- or who said it meant there could be some auxiliary shelling of that area, which happened from time to time, not too often, but it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if this underground command post had windows?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No. My impression is there were no windows. My impression is it was underground, but I didn't check this specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long were you in this command post?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I would believe ten minutes perhaps; maybe 15, I don't know. But it was a not a long stay, but it was not rushed, so we could go around and look and talk about different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also told us that you saw a fax at this location. On how many occasions did you ever send any kind of faxes to the 3rd Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: In the beginning, before my leave in Split, I never used fax. I didn't know they had eventually fax. I don't know if they had it. Afterwards at least once I used fax. I would say it was not used too often, because we, the ECMM, didn't have a fax, so I used the fax of the UNHCR office when I faxed to 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the status of land-line telephones within the area that you monitored.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: My impression is that inside the Zenica region - and with that I mean down to Kiseljak, down to Visoko, up north to Tesanj - the PTT that worked often -- not always, definitely not always -- inside the Zenica area. The city of Zenica and the villages around, it worked more often, but definitely not every time. And when we were to phone, for instance, 3rd Corps, we knew that we needed to be prepared if the phone didn't work to go with a message by car to HQ 3rd Corps. So it was no efficient communication means to us or to others using the PTT net. That was what they said in the hotel where we were accommodated, as well as UNHCR told us. Concerning communication to, for instance, Sarajevo, our opinion, because the information was that there were no PTT line at all there were no possibility to phone with normal telephone to or from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than this communication equipment that you saw in the underground command post, were you aware of any other communications systems or means of communication that the senior leadership of the 3rd Corps had at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I didn't see any equipment myself. I know that at some occasion Mr. Merdan told me that Mr. Hadzihasanovic was called to some meeting with supreme commanders in Sarajevo. And I asked how he could get it, because according to my belief there was no possibility to use the land line, the PTT. So I asked if they had other means of communication, for instance, satellite phones. He -- Mr. Merdan said no, they didn't have, but they had some means of communication by air. What that was he didn't say, or he didn't want to say and he didn't say it. And this was, if I say so, in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point later in your deployment or even into the subsequent NordBat deployment, did anyone from 3rd Corps ever provide you with any kind of telephone numbers that you could use?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, when I was senior liaison officer in NordBat in 1993/1994, occasionally I saw Mr. Hadzihasanovic and some other high-ranking BiH army commanders in Hotel Tuzla, which I visited because I had some matters with the ECMM in Tuzla, having their HQ in this building. And at that time I went to Mr. Hadzihasanovic and said hello and said that -- presented myself via the interpreter that I had this situation with senior liaison officer in NordBat in Tuzla region. Also I said I had intention to go to Zenica to visit 3rd Corps because we had some liaison needs. And I got from Mr. Hadzihasanovic - at that time General Hadzihasanovic - or through some adjutant to him a satellite telephone number so I could call 3rd Corps to arrange this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, did you ever attempt to communicate with 3rd Corps via this phone number that you were provided?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I did so, but it didn't work. If I did it only once or twice, I'm not sure, but it didn't work, so I used another means of communication through the UNPROFOR lines, via BritBat, to come in contact with the 3rd Corps, which worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, based on your encountered and meetings with General Hadzihasanovic, were you able to form any kind of an opinion as to his military professionalism?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. I think I got an opinion - if it's correct or not, not too easy to say - but my impression of General Hadzihasanovic was that he was as a commander 3rd Corps a professional officer. He was calm. He never became irritated or surprised when we had meetings and we passed informations or questions. He always kept a balanced manner. He gave the impression of being in control of the situation, or at least he didn't want to show us he wasn't. He had in general a positive appearance to us. He never used any hard words, at least what we heard through the interpreter. But I think it was no hard words; it should, I think, have been seen in his face. A very professional, balanced officer, having control of the situation. That's my short opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'd like to turn now to your second deployment to Bosnia. You told us earlier that following the ECMM deployment you returned to your regiment. Do you recall approximately when you received information or orders that you would be redeploying to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: My regiment -- and the brigade commander of that regiment, it's a special organisation in Sweden, got the orders to organise the 1st Nordic Battalion in April 1993, just after I had returned from Bosnia. And the preparations started with staff work, and that means that when I returned and got some leave, I was involved in these preparations from, I would say, early May. At that time, we didn't know to which part of the former Yugoslavia this battalion should go, and this battalion consisted of the main part Swedish and the Danish tank company. It was supported by a Norwegian field hospital and the Norwegian helicopter unit too. But we started the preparation, the training of the officers in May. And I took part, of course, in that because I had some experience of at least Central Bosnia and the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when did you find out where you would be going in Bosnia for this second deployment?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I think it was -- I don't know exactly, but in early August. Up to then, we didn't know, and UNPROFOR most probably hadn't decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was the battalion that you were assigned to stationed when you did in fact deploy?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't catch your question exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When your battalion did deploy to Bosnia, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Okay. We went to the Tuzla region, and the battalion was deployed with the HQ company in what we called the factory building, west-south-west of Tuzla, north of Zavidovici, with one company next to the Tuzla air field south of it, with one company up to Srebrenik, north-north-west of Tuzla; and with one company to the Vares area, deployed in some fabric building just east of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "fabric building," do you -- can you elaborate on what that was, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Well, I may be not using the right word. I mean an industrial building. It was some industry. I don't know exactly what they had done Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. earlier, but it was closed down, and it was located on the road from Vares, direction east, after having passed through a rather long tunnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, who was the commander of the Nordic Battalion that you deployed with?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: The commander of the Nordic Battalion was Colonel Ulf Henricsson, who was normally the brigade commander of the training brigade of my regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, what was the time period that you were deployed with NordBat in the Tuzla region?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That was in September. We -- part of the battalion HQ, with the commander of course, made a recce tour some days before, and then we left with the battalion from Denmark, where we had the final training in a training area in the south-west of Denmark, and we went by car on the road all the way through Hungary and via the place -- or base next to Belgrade. So we came into our area of responsibility via Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Sorry, I've forgotten the date. I have it in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What's the approximate month and year?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That was in, I would say, late September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long were you in the Tuzla area?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I stayed with the battalion up to mid-April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you say you arrived in late September, was the full Nordic Battalion deployed and on the ground in the region by late September 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No. It was not. We had some problems in deploying all of the battalion, especially the Danish tank company didn't arrive until spring 1994 because the Serbian government didn't allow the company to go via Serbia, via Bosnian-Serb-held territory in Zvornik. So they had after months in Serbia to go another way, to Venice and then by boat to Split, and then by road from Split up to Tuzla. So they stayed most of that time waiting, waiting, waiting for coming to the deployment area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, can you briefly tell us, first of all, where you physically, you yourself personally, were physically stationed and what your duties were as a senior liaison officer during this NordBat deployment.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I was a part of the battalion HQ, and I was accommodated together with the other staff officers in this, what we called the factory building. My normal place for work were around, meeting different parts. And my tasks were to have liaison with the 2nd Corps BiH army, also with the different operational groups under the command of 2nd Corps, also with the HVO units existing. There was some brigade unit from HVO in the Tuzla region under the control, they said, of commander 3rd Corps -- sorry, commander 2nd Corps. Also, I had the responsibility to have normal contacts with the political establishment in Tuzla region, mainly the mayor of Tuzla, Mr. Beslagic. Also with the president of the regional government. I've forgotten his name, but the contacts with him were very few. Also, I maintained some contacts with the different religious leaders in Tuzla region, especially to mention is that we tried to have a contact with the remaining part of the Serb Orthodox Church in Tuzla region. The bishop, he had left, but there were a contact person or some contact persons. Also, I had the responsibility for normal liaison with the other international organisations in this area: UNHCR, with all of their different non-governmental organisations, as well as with ICRC, having an office in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Torping.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, also I had some contacts with different mayors of other cities, for instance in Zavidovici, because there were some troubles from time to time there. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Torping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. President. Just for Your Honours and for the Defence, I note that I will take about 10 to 15 minutes to complete the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is half past 10.00. We shall resume around five to 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And for the record, as the witness was returning, he attempted to speak to me before I could tell him to stop and the usher could put him in the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise for that, but as I explained to you yesterday, once you've taken the declaration, neither party is allowed to speak with you. But I will give you the opportunity, if there was -- if what you wanted to say was to clarify a previous answer, I will certainly give you the opportunity to do that right now.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to say, because I clarified my memory with my notes. The battalion arrived late September 1993 to Tuzla region, namely the 30th of September. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us immediately before the break that you in your capacity as senior legal officer with NordBat met with the commander of the 2nd Corps of the Bosnian army. Do you recall the name of that individual?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I just have to say I was senior liaison officer, not legal officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: The name of commander 2nd Corps at that time was Hazim Sadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, you've also told us that one of the NordBat companies was in Vares. Do you know which corps of the ABiH, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, had responsibility for Vares?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, we didn't know exactly. There were some different opinions. And I can't give an exact answer because of that. But it was in the area between 2nd and 3rd Corps. Our opinion was that it was 2nd Corps responsibility. But to say also is that concerning the HVO organisation, the HVO brigade in Vares, according to our information, was under the command and hopefully control of HVO commander Central Bosnia, Blaskic. So it was not an exact situation concerning the different borders, according to our opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, do you recall if you had any discussions with any senior Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina military leaders about this issue?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: As far as I remember, when we first time had a meeting with corps commander of 2nd Corps, we informed about our deployment, also the company in the Vares area, and then we discussed this matter. And I think I got that answer that it was more or less 2nd Corps responsibility, but I'm not remembering the wording exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, you also told us shortly before the break about HVO units that were part of the 2nd Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct. It was a brigade or what was called a brigade, HVO brigade, in the -- sorry, in the Tuzla area, and that was under the control of 2nd Corps BiH army. Also, I would say maybe that the Chief of Staff 2nd Corps at that time was a Bosnian Croat, Maka [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, if you know, can you explain to the Trial Chamber why it was that the 2nd Corps had HVO units within it.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I think the situation in North-East Bosnia, the Tuzla region, as we called it, was not the same ethnically, politically, as in Central Bosnia. In the north-east part, the Tuzla region, the Bosnian Croats were much fewer, according to our opinion and knowledge, compared to in Central Bosnia. They were weaker, and because of that they didn't believe they had a chance to be as independent, if I call it independent, as in Central Bosnia with the Bosnian Croat-dominated, Vitez, and so on. They were in the Tuzla region more loyal to the Bosnian government and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the 2nd Corps because of the real situation in that region. That's our opinion in NordBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, I'd like to draw your attention to the first few days of November 1993. During the first few days of that month, can you tell us about any discussions or communications you had with the commander of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: This was, I think, the 6th or maybe 8th of November. And in the Vares area, there were fighting and the situation was not clear at all. I was in the Tuzla region. The battalion commander, Colonel Henricsson himself, was in the Vares area. I was called by CO 2nd Corps, and he passed a demand or a wish. He wanted NorBat to redeploy from its present deployment to the area between 2nd Corps and 3rd Corps to, as he expressed it, try to stop the looting of 7th Muslimanski Brigade, which according to information we had was a part definitely of 3rd Corps, and fighting in the area of Vares and east of Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me attempt to clarify one thing that you've said earlier, sir. At this point in time you were not in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Not personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us that the 7th Muslim or Muslimanski Brigade, as you put it, was definitely part of 3rd Corps. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: How, I don't know exactly. It was stated that it was a part of 3rd Corps; I can't recall why. I presume that was information from 8th Company, our battalion in Vares, but also we had that information in the BH command, UNPROFOR documents concerning fighting factions, different units, and since long 7th Muslimanski Brigade was told to be a part the mobile unit of 3rd Corps. That's the reason I stated it was a part of 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, during the time you had previously been in Central Bosnia, that is, when you were an ECMM monitor in the first few months of 1993, what corps did the 7th Muslim Brigade belong to then?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It belonged, according to our opinion in the ECMM and Team Zenica, to 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us a moment ago that the 7th Muslim Brigade was a part of the mobile unit of 3rd Corps. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I believe the part of 3rd Corps which was mobile. I would say that most of BiH army units, both during my ECMM period but also when I was with NorBat, were, if I call it, Territorial Defence units deployed normally along the front line between Bosnian-government- controlled area and by Bosnian-Serb-controlled area. Then they had part of the units home; for instance, a brigade in Zavidovici had a part of the frontier, and they sent soldiers maybe weekly or monthly to the front and replaced the other ones in that brigade. But our opinion concerning 7th Muslimanski Brigade was that that brigade didn't have any own part of the front against the Bosnian Serbs; it was a unit possible to use where and when needed, and it consisted of several battalions recruited in different parts of Central Bosnia. There was a part in Zenica, a part in Travnik, a part, I think, in Kladanj, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, you told us a few moments ago about this discussion you had in November with the commander of the 2nd Corps. Do you recall asking him the basis of the information he was relaying to you or how he knew this information?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I presumed if he passed this information and this wish, he had, so to say, sufficient information. I didn't ask him in what way he had got it and so on. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what did you do with that information you received from the 2nd Corps ABiH commander?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I passed this information by radio to the battalion commander down in Vares, and he was in the middle of it. He said - and it was a real mess in Vares and east of violations of the -- Vares - and he said there were no possibilities for NorBat to redeploy immediately and to solve this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to return now to the final few questions I'd like to ask you. After this event in Vares, did you have any other communication with anyone from the 3rd Corps of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, referring to what I said earlier concerning I got the telephone number from General Hadzihasanovic in Hotel Tuzla, that was just some days after these events, if I remember correctly. And after that I had two visits during the rest of my tour in Zenica to cooperate and have liaison with the 3rd Corps, as well as I met Colonel Blaskic in HVO HQ in Vitez, because of -- we had the Vares area, which was under the control of HVO Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Torping, on these occasions or at this occasion in Hotel Tuzla, do you recall what you spoke to General Hadzihasanovic about?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It was a very short, if I -- I shouldn't call it a meeting, but we met. I said hello and presented myself as being now the senior liaison officer to NorBat, and also I said I had the intention to visit 3rd Corps in Zenica, among others, or mainly because of we could have some interest in the Vares area where we had a company and most probably 3rd Corps had the responsibility from BiH army point of view. But I don't remember exactly the wording of that. And as I said earlier, General Hadzihasanovic gave a positive appearance and said yes, and to arrange this meeting he passed to me this telephone number for what I understood was a satellite telephone. Then I left because -- I saw the president, Izetbegovic, was appearing and I think I had no reason to remain there when high-ranking Bosnian personalities were gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So is it clear from your answer, sir, that President Izetbegovic arrived at the Hotel Tuzla while you were present?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: He was in the hotel, and I think I saw him coming down some stairs. So this was in the lobby ground floor. Obviously he had been some floor up before. Also, the major, Mr. Beslagic, came at the same time. If they had had some meeting or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Shortly after this event in Tuzla, did you have any further contact with senior leadership of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to use this telephone number to arrange with this meeting, and it didn't work, as I said earlier. So I tried to arrange a contact via UNPROFOR BritBat in Vitez, and it succeeded. So me myself, as well as the company commander of 8th Company, Major Hakan Birger - some other also was present - we left for Zenica and had a meeting in Zenica with General Hadzihasanovic -- no, with at that time the CO of 3rd Corps, Mr. - or was it General at that time, I don't know - Alagic. Also at that time in the HQ building, when we had the meeting with Mr. Alagic -- or sorry, General Alagic, General Hadzihasanovic entered that room, so we met him there too in his function as Chief of Staff, I understand. Chief of Staff, BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall the approximate date you had this meeting with General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: If I don't remember wrong, it was in the beginning of December. But sorry, I do not have the date in my head. I have it in my papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Torping, what year would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the topics of conversation with General Alagic at this meeting in the beginning of December 1993?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. Because that was the first time we - me myself and the company commander of Vares NorBat - met him. We presented ourselves, and the deployment of NorBat and said that we had an interest of having a calm situation in that area, which obviously at this situation -- in the situation was controlled by 3rd Corps. And what I remember, what he said was that there will be no problem in that area. Yeah, that was what we discussed. I think when that had been said -- I'm not sure exactly, but I think in this phase of the meeting General Hadzihasanovic entered the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. room. And then came some social talk of that -- because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Two last questions, sir: Where was this meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It was held in the HQ building 3rd Corps, and that room which -- what I understood was the room of commander 3rd Corps. I believe it was the same room as we had had meetings with Mr. Hadzihasanovic earlier, but I'm not exactly clear of that. But it was in that building and in the room of CO 2nd -- sorry, 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And finally, sir, just to clarify: This meeting that you had with General Alagic, you said that you discussed having an interest in having a calm situation in that area. What area were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: The area of Vares, which was of common interest to us, NorBat, and to 3rd Corps. The Vares area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Torping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As the examination-in-chief is over, I give the floor to the Defence for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel Torping. We met already yesterday, and I wish to thank you for giving representatives of the Defence a chance to discuss the events which you could be a witness and which happened during your mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina. For the record, I will introduce myself once again. I am Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Hadzihasanovic. I will have a few questions for you in connection with the topics and events that you were asked about by my learned friend. After some training, you arrived in Zenica on the 26th or 27th of December, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the European Monitoring Mission had three teams: One deployed in Tuzla; another one in Zenica; and a third in Tomislavgrad. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct, concerning this area of course. There were others in Knin, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Bosnia and Herzegovina now. All three teams were actually subordinated to the regional centre located in Split in a neighbouring state, that is, the Republic of Croatia. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Answering a question from my learned friend, you told us that your area of responsibility or where you performed your mission was very large, going in the north from Konjic, Tarcin, Kiseljak, Breza, Kakanj, Maglaj, Tesanj; in the west Turbe and Travnik; and south as far as Gornji Vakuf, including Vitez, Busovaca, Fojnica, Visoko, and Tomislavgrad. Is that right? Was that your area?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That was correct, except not Tomislavgrad. That was that other team in Tomislavgrad.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding right that your area in the north and in the west and partially in the east was delineated by the confrontation lines between the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you knew, Colonel, that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the legitimate armed force of the State of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which had already become a member of the United Nations. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have told us, during your mission, from the 25th of March in 1993, you didn't have occasion to go into the area under the control of the VRS because the VRS would not allow European monitors to perform their mission in territory under their control; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I would say that we in Team Zenica couldn't come into -- or penetrate the line of confrontation. We were not accepted on the other side. They shot at us. If there were other teams in the territory of the Bosnian Serbs, I'm not exactly sure, but there were no other teams near the confrontation line on the Bosnian Serb side; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. You have already described in detail that as members of the European mission you were interested in grasping the social, political, and security situation in the area and that for that reason from the very beginning you established contact with the civilian, political, religious, and military officers in the area. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have described in detail all the meetings that you had, and you met the commander of the 3rd Corps at the beginning of January 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct. I think 3rd of January.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the first meeting you had with the officers and commander of the 3rd Corps, you were able to note that the 3rd Corps and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina have an extremely positive attitude towards the Monitoring Mission and immediately expressed their willingness to cooperate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: They expressed directly willingness to cooperate and a positive attitude to us. That's our opinion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, because of the seriousness of the situation and the need to fully perform your function, towards the end of February the regional centre that was responsible for the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed in Zenica, and its first leader was the French diplomat Jean-Pierre Thebault; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct. Ambassador Thebault.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already said that in executing your duties you would frequently be in the field together with representatives of the army and HVO, and you were able to see on the ground how the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was organised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It's right from that point of view that when the joint commission was organised, we in the commission including BiH army and HVO representatives were going together in the field. Before that, the team -- the team leader and me myself and then with another monitor -- we went around in the field and we got some impression of the situation. Definitely. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that when you arrived in Zenica, in your judgement the situation was quite peaceful. However, is it right, Colonel, that shortly after that, that is, sometime in mid-January, there were open conflicts between the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Croatian Defence Council in the areas of Novi Travnik, Gornji Vakuf, and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct. And I would say in the Gornji Vakuf area it started slightly before the problems - if I call them problems - came to the Busovaca area. The Gornji Vakuf area were more tense earlier than the other areas you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as you became aware of armed conflicts in Gornji Vakuf, you attempted to get in touch with the command of the 3rd Corps and to learn from them what they could do; however, your impression from that period was that the 3rd Corps Command had very poor links and knew very little about what was happening in Gornji Vakuf and that the army units in Gornji Vakuf were relatively independent in their combat operations. Was that what you learnt?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
