utterances.text: I would express it like this: We understood, me and my teammate, that the possibilities to get the information from Gornji Vakuf were slightly limited and maybe it was some difficulties for the commander of 3rd Corps to directly get orders to the sub-commanders. But we were not too sure of this situation. In general, it seemed very complicated and difficult situation. So I can't state that there were very limited resources, but I can accept the wording "limited resources." Definitely, yes. It was not an easy situation for the corps commander 3rd Corps, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you could see while observing members of the BiH army and comparing them with the Croatian Defence Council was that they were not as well equipped, that not all the troops had weapons, that some soldiers didn't have uniforms or had only parts of the uniforms. So your conclusion was that the HVO at that point in time was stronger than the BiH army. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I would say the word "stronger" I am not sure. But they -- the separate units gave an impression being better dressed, better equipped, and better managed. If the conclusion of that totally is, they - HVO - was stronger than 2nd -- sorry, 3rd Corps, I have no opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am not going to ask you about the Joint Busovaca Commission, because you have spoken in great detail about its position, establishment, and tasks. However, I wish to ask you the following: Is it correct that when you went on field missions together with the Deputy Commander Merdan, you could see that local commanders wanted to be independent in their combat operations and they were reluctant in obeying commands from their superiors and that very often Deputy Merdan took a lot of time and effort in order to convince local commanders to obey orders? Would that be the knowledge that you got from the personal contacts that you had?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. In general, I would say that the problems we faced often was passing through checkpoints. I had believed when we had a high-ranking 3rd Corps representative, the deputy, as well as Chief of Staff HVO Central Bosnia, it shouldn't be too difficult to pass the checkpoints. But we had often problems. And of course when we should pass the checkpoint manned by a unit of the 3rd Corps and we were not allowed immediately to pass, I asked Mr. Merdan to explain to them the situation and, if possible, order them to open the checkpoint. And what I could understand and see, he really tried hard to do so. Sometimes he succeeded; sometimes not. And that gave me the impression that local commanders, different levels, were not too happy to obey orders from their own higher ranking officers. Why could be discussed; it's to say that sometimes we got the answer when I asked the interpreter what the local commander said, they said, "We can't contact our commander. And without our commander's admission, you can't pass, even if it's some high-ranking person from above." They gave the impression of trying to be, as you mentioned, independent. It was not easy to convince them that this was the order of the high levels of 3rd Corps. What is to say also is that Mr. Merdan had, as no one in BiH army at that time, what I understand, no ranks. They had just a badge stating they belonged to BiH army, the governmental army. He had no identification card as well as was the situation for HVO, no identification cards either. So it was not too easy, maybe, for a local commander if he didn't recognise the face of this person, to believe this is a high-level officer. And this was a practical part. But definitely it was difficult and I think Mr. Merdan did what he could do to convince them that it was an activity definitely accepted by and supported by the corps commander 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already stated that Commander Hadzihasanovic and his deputy, Merdan, were professional, good soldiers and that they did what they could do in such situations. Would you agree with me that it was the period of time when they did their utmost to discipline the troops and to create a professional army; however, that the chain of command at that time was not fully established and that for that reason you encountered the problems that you have just described to us?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I'm not in the situation I can judge if they did their utmost to discipline their units, so I can't answer that question in that way. I can say that there were no indications, as far as I could see, when I met Mr. Hadzihasanovic and when I worked together with Mr. Merdan, that they should ignore these parts of the command. But I was not in that position I could judge so generally as you expressed it. I understand they had a difficult task in a difficult situation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have also said that in your conversation with Commander Hadzihasanovic you had the impression - or at least this is the impression that he wanted to create - was that he was in control of the situation, that he had the upper hand. Would you agree with me that it would be normal for a commander to try and create an impression that he controlled the situation because he is aware that this fact would have an impact on you in your position, as well as on representatives of other international organisations, and that the word would spread? Also, this impression that he controlled the situation was important for him because of his main mission and the message that this would convey to the enemy. And even if he hadn't controlled the situation, he wanted to convey this message that he did have the upper hand. Would that be a normal role that a commander would wish to play, as far as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: In general, I think that's a normal way. I would add maybe that my impression is that Mr. Hadzihasanovic in the later part of my period gave more the impression of controlling the situation compared to the first part, the first weeks of my tour. If that depends on that the situation for 3rd Corps improved during this period of three months or not, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answering my learned friend's questions, you spoke about several occasions when you get by -- got by some information and you wanted to check this information. The first such case was the information that you had received from the mayor of Vitez, a Bosnian Croat. According to him, there were 2.000 Mujahedins in the area. Is it true, Colonel, that you paid a visit not only to this army unit in Travnik but that you also went to other areas mentioned by the mayor; meaning the areas north of Vitez, and then you went to the areas east of Zenica? You wanted to locate these Mujahedins, however, you could not get hold of any evidence about the presence of Mujahedins in the 3rd Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That is correct. And I can say that I -- after the visit to Travnik, we - I think the next day - left for checking the area east of Zenica, east of the river, and also had some short discussions with UNHCR if they had seen something, and there were no real information. It was only that, some few rumours. And we checked part of the area east of Zenica, didn't find anything. We returned to Zenica, and then we dove to the area north of Vitez, where this Bosnian Croat mayor of Vitez had pointed out it should be a lot of Mujahedin fighters. We drove a lot, for a long distance, until we came what we believed near the confrontation-line area, where we met a position of BH army people and we asked them, and they said there were no foreign fighters, no Mujahedin. They belonged to the unit of the 7th Muslimanski Brigade, and they didn't allow us to go further because they said it was dangerous and, as a matter of fact, we said we can go ourselves, but they didn't allow us, and we returned. But we during this period didn't find any evidence of any, if I say so, real foreign fighters, Mujahedin, in 3rd Corps area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just repeat, Colonel Torping. You raised this issue with Commander Hadzihasanovic and then with Mr. Merdan and other officers. All of them and all the foot soldiers clearly told you that there were no Mujahedins in any of the units of the 3rd Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Concerning the foot soldiers, I don't know. But concerning the officers, Mr. Hadzihasanovic, Mr. Merdan, and other commanders, they stated there were no foreign soldiers in 3rd Corps; it was just, as they said, local Bosnian soldiers. Concerning the foot soldiers, we didn't discuss with them too much and we didn't get any real answer concerning this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought that in Travnik and north of Vitez you had spoken with some soldiers who told you the same. Maybe I didn't understand you correctly. Did you indeed say that these soldiers told you that there were no foreigners amongst them? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Okay. You are referring maybe when -- to the situation when we drove from Vitez direction north towards the confrontation line to this BiH position. It was a platoon or something like that. We talked to what I believe was the local commander, and he said there were no foreign soldiers in the units there. But if that complied [sic] to all of 3rd Corps, I don't know. But in that area he stated "no foreign fighters."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When describing a meeting that you had with Commander Hadzihasanovic, you told us that at that meeting you discussed a threat issued by Colonel Blaskic that he would shell Zenica if the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina continued to reinforce its troops. Do you remember that particular meeting and that particular conversation?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I think it was mid-January, maybe 15th, 17th of January, and it was a message from HVO Colonel Blaskic that they, HVO, should shell Zenica; that means the town, or city of Zenica, I presume. If the reinforcement of BiH army units, 3rd Corps, of course, in the area north of Busovaca and Vitez, I presume, continued to increase, because the opinion of HVO - and I think that was correct - was that the units of 3rd Corps had increased in that area. And this was a response obviously from HVO. And that matter we discussed with Mr. Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have just consulted your statement, and I can see that this conversation took place on the 25th of January. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that two days later you heard shelling from the direction of Busovaca to the south-west of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Well, if the day is 25th, in my statement that is correct, yes. Concerning the shelling, it happened -- if it was one or two days after, I don't remember exactly, but just after. And that we were the Team Zenica in Zenica and we heard in the morning - I think it was around 11.00 - approximately 20 explosions, and we found out with our experience it should be explosions of shells, and that the sound of these explosions was in direction south, direction Busovaca from Zenica. From where these shells were shot, we couldn't find out at all, but the shelling was south of Zenica, direction Busovaca, and that could be a connection to this threat from Blaskic soldiers. We don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: According to what you know, there really was fighting going on in that area, and given the sound of shelling, you could have concluded that there was fighting in that area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: At that exact time, that day, I didn't know if there was some fighting in that direction, south of the city of Zenica. But I was not astonished and because the shelling, I believed, there were some fighting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at your statement, I can see that on that same day you were invited by the HVO from Zenica and you were told that allegedly in three villages east of Busovaca 14 Croats had been killed and that they were transported to the hospital in Zenica and that their friends and families, people who had left the area, were also in Zenica and they asked for assistance with their transportation to Vitez. Is that what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I said approximately that, but it was so that the local HDZ HVO in Zenica phoned us and told us that there had been 14 Croats, Bosnian Croats, captured and after that killed in three villages, no names given, small villages east of Busovaca, and that the corpses were transported to the hospital of Zenica and these people from HDZ HVO wanted us to go to the hospital to control the condition of the corpses. Also, they said that some relatives to these killed persons, refugees at present, had left -- had had to leave the villages and were transported to Zenica, and it was approximately one load -- bus load. And they were at present accommodated with Bosnian Croat friends and relatives in Zenica, but they wanted these refugees to be transported safely out of Zenica as fast as possible to Vitez, and that was the subject for a meeting with the corps commander 3rd Corps that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The reason for which you spoke to Commander Hadzihasanovic was to ask for the 3rd Corps assistance in transporting these families safely to Vitez and in burying the bodies of those people who had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It's correct that we presented the problem and said that it's needed for safe transport of these people to Zenica -- sorry, from Zenica to Vitez, as well as decent burial of the corpses, because that was what the HDZ HVO had asked for. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, during your conversation with Commander Hadzihasanovic, you never told him what the HDZ told you about the alleged killing of these people. You never told him where these people were allegedly killed. The only thing you mentioned was that you needed his assistance with the transportation of these families and the burial of the bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I gave the story that they were killed. I didn't know the names of the villages, so I couldn't pass it to corps commander. And the most important thing in this situation was to solve the problem with the refugees. That's correct. So that was what I, we, concentrated on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The commander provided you with all the requested assistance. He only asked you to inspect these people before they left to see whether they had any arms on them. This was indeed done, and these people left Zenica safely, after having been inspected for arms.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's not exactly correct, but in reality, yes. The corps commander was positive for the transport of these people to Vitez; no problem with that. But he said that they could have some weapons and because of that it was needed to check this. And he said, if I remember correctly, that 3rd Corps military police can check that. I said that they were very afraid, these people, and if they had some weapons and 3rd Corps military police should come and check them, it could be very hostile and they were very afraid. And then corps commander, what I can remember, said, "Okay, then we can combine a military police patrol of both 3rd Corps military police and some HVO military police from the HVO brigade in Zenica. " And that was to me a good solution. So I said I will pass this to HDZ HVO as well as I passed it to ICRC. Also, when I passed it, I said the day after, because it was late, we, the team, should go to the hospital to check the bodies, because the HDZ HVO stated it could be so they were mutilated or something like that. But the next day we got another order creating a joint commission, so we never had the time, chance, to go to the hospital. And what I understand concerning the transport to Vitez, it worked; otherwise, I'd have got some report concerning that. So I think it worked without any complaints. But I do not know. I didn't get a report stating that. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When talking to Commander Hadzihasanovic, you told him that you had been provided with this information by the HDZ, that the bodies were in the hospital; however, you didn't tell him what your intentions were. You didn't tell him what you were going to do next during that conversation that you had with him.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct. Because I didn't at that time knew exactly what the next step should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you remained there up to the 25th of March with a 15-day break, you remained in Zenica; that is, your numerous tasks prevented you from returning and re-addressing that issue and from checking whether the events unfolded in the way you were told by the HDZ. In other words, you did not spend any time investigating this incident.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't do it myself, because of the day after this situation, we in Zenica was ordered to form a joint commission for cease-fire, and that was organised with representatives of the BiH army, Mr. Merdan, and HVO, Mr. Nakic. And I believe, as a matter of fact, one of the issues at the meeting - which could be the 28th or 29th of January, 1993, I don't remember exactly - was we discussed this matter. And if I remember correctly we found out together, including the HVO members, that this matter was not of highest priority compared to other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. matters to deal with in that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you can remember, during that meeting and at the request of the HVO, Mr. Merdan provided a certain report about the information that the army had as to what was going on in the area and how the persons mentioned were killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No, sorry, I do not know. But it could also be so that I was personally not present all time of this meeting. I had some other matter also. So maybe my teammate in this commission was chairing that part. I do not know. But that report was never mentioned to me. I have no idea of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though the cease-fire agreement concluded at the end of January had envisaged freedom of movement, in answer to questions from my learned friend you said that you transported Deputy Merdan and other officers of the 3rd Corps on a daily basis from Zenica, who had come to attend joint commission meetings. Is it right that during your tour of duty members of the Armija did not have freedom of movement through the areas controlled by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's my opinion, and definitely it was not safe for members of BiH army in the joint commission to go themselves into the area of Busovaca, which was HVO-controlled. That was not safe. So we had to protect them by this transportation service. And I would say the same when we were out in the terrain; we normally used either Danish armoured personnel carriers, as I described before the break, or British armoured personnel carriers to provide security to the members of the joint commission when we were in HVO-held area for the BiH part, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned an incident arousing dissatisfaction by members of the HVO when they saw that a member of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was in your vehicle and when Mr. Nakic had to invest a great deal of effort to avoid an incident from breaking out.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your sojourn in Bosnia and Herzegovina, you are aware that the Bosniak population was expelled in large numbers from Kiseljak and Busovaca and in order to have the people returned to their homes, you had a meeting with Dario Kordic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I had a meeting with Mr. Kordic, yes. That was one of the subjects. There were other subjects too. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your proposal was that the local authorities assist in repairing houses so that people could go back to their homes, and Dario Kordic told you on that occasion that they would repair the houses of Bosnian Croats but not those of Bosnian Muslims, because those who had been expelled should not come back. Is that what you learnt during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I don't remember exact wording, but that's the general message, yes. Mr. Kordic was not positive at all for repatriation of Bosnian Muslim families and persons into the present HVO HDZ-held areas. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you referred to one of your visits to the 3rd Corps; that is, in the former administrative building of the Zenica ironworks, when Commander Hadzihasanovic took you to the basement of that building and showed you the communications centre and the operations centre. When you arrived in the basement, were you told that these were premises built by the Zenica ironworks as a nuclear shelter for that particular administrative building?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That, I can't remember. What I can remember is, but not the wording, that it was built or it was corrected to be shellproof. But what purpose, I can't remember, was given to me. No. But it could be so, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw radio stations there. Did you take a closer look to see what kind of radio stations they were?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No, I didn't took a closer look because of it was a social visit. I didn't want to misuse the hospitality of Mr. Hadzihasanovic. Also, I am not an expert of Yugoslavian radio stations, so I couldn't get too much knowledge. But I understood they were rather many and of different types -- that means for different purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that these were not military radio stations but amateur radio stations of Kenwood and BICOM brands, would you agree with me that such radio stations for such wartime conditions were not reliable and they were not are reliable communications system for wartime?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I think I saw this type of stations you mentioned also, but I can remember also, what I saw, some military radio stations. Concerning the capacity for these stations, you mentioned for military purposes; I do not know. But if they are useful for peacetime, they should have some use during wartime too, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What you saw and what you learnt from contacts with the 3rd Corps could lead you to conclude that the 3rd Corps was in communication with the Supreme Command, but on the basis of that information you cannot testify as to the quality of the communications between the 3rd Corps and subordinate brigades and units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct. I can't have any contact opinion of that, no. That's correct, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If communication with subordinate units depended on ground links, then you will agree that such PTT links were often down and that they did not ensure reliable communications.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct. They were for us, and I presume for 3rd Corps also, as others, unreliable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The offer of Commander Hadzihasanovic and the invitation for you to visit the communications centre and the operations centre was of significance to you because it was a demonstration of the confidence that the corps commander had in the Monitoring Mission, as he was showing premises which usually an army would keep secret; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The enemy forces to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is, the HVO, never showed you any such premises or facilities.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your tour of duty in Bosnia and Herzegovina as a member of the Monitoring Mission, there were discussions about a political settlement to the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was the period when the Vance-Owen Plan was a current topic of discussion. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I'm not now exactly sure of timing of the Vance-Owen Plan. I haven't checked in my notes, because this was on a much higher level than I worked as a monitor. So I can't answer yes or no to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from my learned friend the Prosecutor, you explained why relations between the HVO in Tuzla and the BH army were different than elsewhere, explaining this by the difference in the situations. Would you agree with me that a certain policy of the HVO and the HDZ in Central Bosnia to have full control over territories which they considered to be historically theirs was also one of the reasons which led to the conflict with the ABiH and the beginning of the offensive against units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Would this be one of the reasons?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes, I think that could be one of the reasons. Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you can remember some details regarding the Vance-Owen Plan discussions, would you agree with me that the proposals for a settlement very frequently did not take into consideration the actual situation on the ground, so that, too, was one of the reasons for the heightening of tensions and subsequently for the conflicts in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I have to say I'm not updated enough to have an answer to that question. Sorry. I can't say either yes or no. And it was not, so to say, a matter for us in the Team Zenica to consider too much. We had much more low-level practical problems to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps just one more question in that area. I don't know to what extent you are -- you know this. Do you know that on the 15th of January the HVO issued an ultimatum to army units to place themselves under command of the HVO within five days and because the units of the BH army rejected this ultimatum, the HVO launched major operations in the area of Donji Vakuf, Novi Travnik, and on the 25th of January also in the area of Busovaca? Were you familiar with these facts at the time, or perhaps subsequently did you learn about them during your mission?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That ultimatum you referred to, I can't remember I was aware of. The fact that fighting started or increased 25th -- around 25th of January I am aware of. But this ultimatum from HVO, I do not know exactly about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have already addressed this matter several times before this Court. I'm just asking you whether during your time there, were you aware that roads were one of the most important issues for the survival of the area and that control of roads was one of the main means of struggle in that period?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I am aware of -- was aware that roads and controlling the roads were very important for the different parties and that from time to time several roads were cut off by one of the parties, yes; with all the consequences for the other it had. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, I hope you will agree if I say that all the problems emanating from the position of the HVO in forcibly implementing the Vance-Owen Plan and all problems linked to the blockade of roads and other problems that the population and the army in the area were confronted with had a decisive impact on the tasks of the commander of the 3rd Corps and he could not neglect them if he wanted to carry out his duty.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I can agree totally in that these problems were of great importance to the commander of the 3rd Corps and he could, of course, not neglect them because of the task he was given to fulfil. No, he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions for this witness. Thank you, Mr. President, that ends my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I give the floor now to the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We only have a few questions for today's witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Torping, could we go back briefly to mid-January, when you visited the headquarters of the Workers Battalion of the 7th Brigade. You came to the battalion headquarters unannounced; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The reason for your visit were the rumours that you had heard about the presence of foreign fighters in the area.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That was the main reason. Of course, we in the team also had an aim to ourselves check the situation in the Travnik-Novi Travnik-Grude area, and the best way to find out was to go around looking yourself, meet people, asking, talking, discussing. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The battalion headquarters was in the centre of town; could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, you spoke to the local commander of the 7th Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: We entered this building where we saw soldiers enter, and we went up to, I think, first or second floor, and we met some soldier coming out of a room. He asked what we were doing. And directly afterwards came another man dressed in uniform - no ranks, and so on - and he presented himself as the instruction officer, the commander, of this unit which I think he said was a battalion of the 7th Muslimanski Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: He told you that the unit consisted exclusively of local soldiers; that is, Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. We asked concerning what unit it was and if he knew anything about the Mujahedin fighter, foreign fighters, and he stated that his unit was a battalion or unit of 7th Muslimanski Brigade and it was only Bosnian soldiers in it, no foreign fighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the events that happened the next day, just to clarify something you said on page 49. When you were in the area of Northern Vitez, you came across members of the 7th Brigade and the local commander you spoke to was also an officer of the 7th Brigade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It was in the terrain north of Vitez, direction confrontation line area, and we came to some platoon or what it was checking the road, and we asked for the commander of that unit and a person came and he said he was the commander. He didn't give any name and so on. He had no rank, they didn't have, but he said he was the chief, the commander on that spot, and that this unit belonged to the 7th Muslimanski Brigade. And we asked if they had seen any Mujahedin fighters or so on, because there were rumours. And he stated that there, in this unit in his area, north of Vitez -- house locally it was, we didn't ask - there were no foreign fighters, no Mujahedin fighters. And he also stated that we couldn't go any further because then it was dangerous because of the BSA, or the Bosnian Serb firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the first time when you visited the battalion headquarters in Travnik and again the next day you didn't find any evidence of the presence of foreign fighters during your tours or inspection or whatever you like to call it?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: During this days, I didn't find any evidence of foreign fighters. And if I understood your question correctly, during my tour, this month up to March 1993, when I was in ECMM, I didn't find any evidence of foreign fighters, Mujahedin fighters, in the area of 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the period when you came to Bosnia again as a member of NordBat. At the beginning of November, you were in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you confirm that while the military operations were ongoing around Vares you didn't travel to Vares, nor were you ever in Vares?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: During that period, I was not in Vares, no, because the battalion commander was there and I had my tasks in the Tuzla area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: The information that you received about problems in Vares came to you from the commander of the 2nd Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: After that, you got in touch with officers of NordBat in Vares and they told you about the problems that they had in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I contacted by radio the battalion commander because this was a direct requisition of the help of NorBat. So he, the battalion commander, Colonel Henricsson, had to take a stand concerning this, and he was in the place or in the area. I passed this wish and message from commander 2nd Corps and Colonel Henricsson said he was on the spot and it was a mess and his judgement was that NorBat 1 Battalion could not solve these problems between 2nd Corps and 3rd Corps. So the result was this request was denied, which I passed to corps commander 2nd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: He confirmed that the situation in Vares was chaotic.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes, he did; in Vares and in the terrain east of Vares, along the road, direction east.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know at that point in time that there were other units in Vares in addition to the 7th Brigade, as well as several thousand civilians?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I knew there were several thousand civilians because that was the population of the town. Some of them, the Bosnian Croats at this situation, refugees; among others, some hundred in the camp or near the camp of 2nd -- sorry, of 8th Company. I was aware of that it was not only 7th Muslim Brigade which had attacked from west direction Vares and east of Vares, but I didn't have any information about that and that was not my interest because of the battalion commander and the information officer of the battalion HQ who were on the spot dealing with these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no further questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, have you any additional questions, as it is half past 12.00 and time for the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no -- no questions at this time for the witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have the break, because the Judges have some questions, and we will resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have some questions to ask you. I am going to give the floor to Judge Swart, who is going to put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I would like to put to you firstly a few questions on the general situation during your first stay in Bosnia, that is, from December 1992 until March 1993. I understand you were among the first monitors from the ECMM in Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I don't know how many were before me, but I think there were very few. And we were just two monitors in Central Bosnia totally, so it could be, but I don't know, maybe three, four others before me, because we had short tours of duty, three -- sorry, three months, normally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You also mentioned the name of Ambassador Thebault. Was he at that time also in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Ambassador Thebault? He became during my period the second head Regional Centre Split, and he went to Zenica, I think, the Regional Centre Zenica was created out of Regional Centre Split last days of January, 30, 31st or something like that and then he came to Zenica some days later. But I was not at that time present, because I had leave from 1st of February to -- I returned to Zenica 17th of February. Then he was there. When he arrived personally in Zenica, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] At that time, did you already have this reporting system that the ECMM developed later on, a system of daily reports mentioning the basic -- the most important facts of the day?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That system existed when I started, and before that, I presume, in very late December 1992. So we had routine of writing down and sending by CAPSAT, our means of communication, a daily report to the centre. I think it should be done before 19 -- 1900 hours each day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So in these reports your main findings would also be included of the period?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The other question I have in this respect: In the first three months of your stay, did you have contact with other international organisations on a regular basis or not?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I had regular contacts with UNHCR in Zenica I would say at least once a week, often depending on the situation, several meetings each week. Also, but not as regularly, I had -- not me personally but the we, the team, had contacts with ICRC head in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That was the International Red Cross or the local one?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No, ICRC, International Red Cross organisation. Concerning the local Red Cross, we had an initial meeting with the head in Zenica, and then I think I met him once or twice when he passed requests concerning help with medicaments and so on to us. But that was not regular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you also have contacts with UNPROFOR, if that was already there at the time?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: There were no UNPROFOR in Zenica, but there was an UNPROFOR part, a BH command with HQ in Kiseljak, as well as some units, the BritBat in Vitez, the French unit in Kladanj, a Canadian unit in Visoko, and the organisation was as such in the BH command in Kiseljak there was a so-called ECLO, a liaison officer of ECMM, as a direct link to the BC command, and we got information from him. We visited often Kiseljak and the HQ of BC command; as well as I visited rather often, especially during the later part of my tour, BritBat in Vitez, as well as I said it was a Dutch-Belge transport battalion with HQ in Busovaca, and we had, when we had our small HQ of the joint commission, next to this Dutch-Belge battalion we had, of course, daily contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If you say daily contacts with UNPROFOR, you probably also include daily exchange of information, or not?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So BritBat would know what you were doing or what were your findings and, on the other hand, you would know what BritBat was doing and what kind of information it had.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I would say that when we had something which could, according to our judgement, be interesting for BritBat, as well as Dutch-Belge battalion, we passed it directly to them. We took part when we wanted in the daily briefings of BritBat, getting information from them as well as from Dutch-Belge battalion, and we had, I would say, nearly a daily contact with the ECLO down in Kiseljak, so we got information from the UNPROFOR BH command. I believe the direction of information from UNPROFOR was slightly greater than in vice versa, because we didn't have as much information as they had totally. But it was to me very positive, open exchange of information. No problem at all with the contacts with the BH command and the units in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the Busovaca Joint Commission was established and it started, if I'm correct, on the 28th of January; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. But at that time, it was called, if I don't remember wrong, the Joint Commission for Cease-fire. But it started in Busovaca. Then it switched name during my leave period to the Joint Commission of Busovaca. Sometimes it was referred to as Joint Commission of Central Bosnia. There were different names, but the same commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And was a cease-fire concluded shortly afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: If I remember correctly now, the 28th of January, 1993, it was an agreement between -- in Vitez between the 2nd Corps -- sorry, the 3rd Corps, of course, and HVO Central Bosnia of a cease-fire, as well as the creation of this joint commission. So it was an agreement signed, if I don't remember wrongly, of both parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you were a member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Not at that time. When I left for my leave the 1st of February, I left Zenica and I didn't know if I should go back after my leave to Zenica or get another position, and when I returned after leave, I stayed with the Regional Centre Split for some days with staff duties before going back to Zenica. Then the idea was I should be an operation officer of the newly created RC Zenica. But I in reality provided myself to the joint commission because it was need of manpower inside that, before I 24th of February got the order to become the next chairman of the joint commission from 25th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: At what date did you become an active participant in the commission, then? Because you said, "I then left Split beginning of February." When did you return?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I returned the 17th of February to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: The 17th.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: But then I, so to say, was a staff member operational officer of the regional centre, but cooperated very intensively with the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you have any active role to play in the establishment of the commission before the 28th? Were you involved in the process or not?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I was partly involved in the process, if I don't remember wrong. The order of organising this joint commission for cease-fire was given the 28th of January, 1993. And then I, as one of the two members of Team Zenica, which was to create this joint commission ECMM part, took part, of course, in the practical preparations, and also I think one of the days - if it was 28th, 29th, or 30th - I was out as ECMM member together with at least Mr. Merdan, Mr. Nakic to solve some local problems in some village. I think that has been discussed earlier here. So I took part in the practical work of the commission before I went for leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: My final question on this matter is: Were other international bodies involved in creating this commission, or was the ECMM the only one?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No. There were discussions briefly before the 28th on a higher level than my level between ECMM and the BH command, UNPROFOR, and my understanding is that the commanding officer of BritBat, Colonel Bob Stewart, he took an active part in these discussions. So I would say it was a joint preparation and decision by ECMM and definitely UNPROFOR, BH command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Would that have been reported in documents that you would get normally?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Would you get information of that negotiation process from BritBat or from any ...?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: The 28th of January. I have to try to recall my memory where I got -- as a matter of fact, the official order came as a message from RC Split, from the ECMM, that we should create this joint commission and cooperate with UNPROFOR units in the area, and we had a direct contact and cooperation with the Dutch-Belge transport battalion concerning mainly the practical administrative matters, because we should be housed in the building next to this battalion. But concerning the operational part, our most important link was to the ops cell of BritBat HQ in Vitez. So we got a lot of detailed information from BritBat, but also of course from BH command in Kiseljak and from RC Split. But the closest link, I would say, direct link was to BritBat in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Do you know by any chance - you mentioned the name of Colonel Stewart as a member of UNPROFOR who was involved in negotiations on a very high level, higher level than yours, on a cease-fire or something - do you know who were the participants from the Croatian and the Bosnian side in that process?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No, I do not have the names of these persons. Colonel Stewart, he was the battalion commander in Vitez, and -- sorry, I can't give you any names concerning that. Most probably it was representatives of the commander 3rd Corps as well as of commander HVO Central Bosnia, Blaskic. But I was not involved or informed of the details concerning these initial discussions before the creation of the joint commission. As a matter of fact, the team leader at that time of Team Zenica was Mr. Jeremy Fleming, a British monitor, and I think he was deeply involved in these discussions, but he ran that business and I ran the business on the field during these days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on a very different topic: You told us about your inquiries with respect to foreign fighters, Mujahedin. You told us that you had raised this issue five times or that your estimate of it with commanding officers of the ABiH army. And you also told us that you made visits to the north of Vitez and the east of Zenica. And when I was listening to you, I was wondering why this enormous interest in the foreign fighters? Why do you go north of Vitez, east of Zenica? Why do you raise this issue five times with the high-ranking officers? What were your reasons for doing so?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: The reasons were several, I would say. The first, maybe not the strongest reason, was the HVO, or the Bosnian Croats, especially in Vitez as well as in Travnik, raised this question and this fear of these foreign, very dangerous soldiers, fighters, with, as they indicated, maybe no command, no control, no normal rules of how to perform the war. Also, as has been said earlier here, the Bosnian government was the legal representatives of the state and, of course, 3rd Corps BiH army was, so to say, the legal army. If there were other armed units, formations with no control or at least not enough control participating in this war, it was important to us to know because we were as monitors tasked to supervise not only the military but also the political situation, so it was, according to our judgement, of great importance to clarify if there were some foreign fighters, Mujahedin fighters, inside our area of responsibility the same as 3rd Corps area of responsibility. But I think, to go back to the first reason, it was a way to -- if we could find evidence there were no foreign fighters, it was a way to calm down the situation, especially for the Bosnian Croat people and, if I say so, disarm some Bosnian Croat leaders who used these rumours as weapons to higher the tension in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: When you went to north of Vitez until you couldn't go further close to the front line, was there a specific reason for going there?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: We were told that in that direction there could be Mujahedin, and this was the most probable road to go to that area. So we, without having any other options, checked that road. That was also the first time I had a chance to look at that area of our area of responsibility, but there were no exact indications there should be anything particular. But it was a chance we took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Do you remember the places where you have been, or is that too much to ask?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: It's too much to answer if I'm just sitting here to give the names. I need a map to clarify that. The only thing I can say, it was Vitez, direction north or north-north-west towards the confrontation line area, and it could have been maybe 10 kilometres or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And who told you that you could find something there?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Who told you to go there?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I think it was this Bosnian Croat mayor of Vitez with his people indicating there could be Mujahedin in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You also told us - and this is a different subject, the last subject I would like to discuss with you - that you were approached in Zenica at the end of January by members of the Croatian community telling you that 14 Croats had been captured and afterwards killed. That's about the words you used. Captured and killed after that, you said.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. That was the information we got, that they were first captured and then killed. And, of course, if they are captured and should be prisoners of war, you are not allowed to kill them; if they are killed during combat, it's quite another thing. But according to this HDZ HVO people, they said these people were captured and then killed, and that should be - if it's correct, which we didn't know - a crime of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: I agree with you there. But my question is first: Did you meet the person who -- or the persons who told this personally, or did you get the information ...?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: We was called by phone and informed of this, and this HDZ person, HVO HDZ, he was both the political and some local defence commander - I don't know exactly - he requested with his other comrades, Croat -- Bosnian Croat comrades, a meeting with us in their building where they had their HDZ HVO office in Central Zenica, and we went to that place and met this person eye to eye with his comrades, and they presented this thing, what they said. But I didn't meet anyone or no one was presented as a refugee from these villages. So it was the, so to say, HDZ people in Zenica giving this information, coming with these requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Do you remember whether they or not told how they obtained the information?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that. But they said that some refugees, approximately a load -- a bus load from these villages, because they talked about three villages, had arrived in Zenica and were accommodated with friends and relatives, Croat -- Bosnian Croat friends, relatives in Zenica. So I presumed they have got the information from these people, but I didn't raise that question specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You just said that if the persons were killed after being captured, that would be a very serious matter, a war crime, you said. How serious did you take the information at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I took the information serious because of if it was so - I didn't know - it should escalate the tense situation even more, and this was in the period -- before, it was rather calm; this was maybe the start of a more tense, hostile situation. So to me it was very important to clarify, if possible, the situation. But even more important was to get rid of the practical information, having these refugees feeling they were threatened in Zenica. If they could be transported to Vitez, that should be good for all parts. And that's the reason I thought this was very important to deal with as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Was that the main reason why you had a talk on the same day with the commander of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Now, you said, when asked about this the following: "I gave the story that they were killed" and then I started to discuss the problem of the refugees. My question is the following: When you say "I gave the story that they were killed," these 14 people, the story that you heard the Croatian people, did this story also include the allegation that they were killed after being captured?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes, that was the information I or we got; they were captured and then killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But my question is whether you told this also to the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's my opinion, I did, yes. But I do not remember exactly the wording when I passed this information or when we passed it, because we were always two; and who said what exactly, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Who was the other person present?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: At that time -- I am not exactly sure if it was maybe so that the new monitor Kees van der Pluijm, a Dutch monitor, had arrived or not. I have to see if I noticed that in my notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you mean anyhow the second representative from the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the commander at that message, of that story?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: What I can remember, he was calm; he didn't react specially. And I think he said he didn't know about the situation. I got the impression after this talk he knew maybe not that 14 or a figure of Croats, Bosnian Croats, were killed, but I got the impression he knew about the fighting, if he was in just these three villages - which maybe wasn't three villages, I don't know exactly - or in the Busovaca area, I do not know. My impression is that when I presented this problem with the refugees we concentrated on that, to try to find a practical solution for that transport, and my impression is that Mr. Hadzihasanovic was positive to solve -- to help to solve the problem. There were some practical things concerning these people could be armed and so on. But I think we found practical solutions. So it was a meet which ended in a positive atmosphere, and after that I went to inform ICRC, because mainly they are the organisation involved concerning refugees to be repatriated and so on and so on. And I also had contacts with HDZ HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: When you left and when the issue of the refugees was settled, did you discuss the event with, if he was already present, with Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No. As far I can remember, when I met Ambassador Thebault, a lot of other things had passed, so this was not too actual. But of course I sent or we sent a daily report to RC Split concerning this situation, so he should be -- or the HQ of RC Split should be aware of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So there would be something in some report from the ECMM on your conversation and on your doings that day.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: There would be, is my question, something reported, in a report of the ECMM on the events that you have told us.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: There should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Your meeting with the Croats, your conversation with the general.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: How detailed, I don't know. But the incident or the situation, I'm quite sure, was in that daily report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You told us also that you were able to organise transport to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was not me organising this transport, because other things happened just afterwards; we got other orders. But what I understand, the transport was organised and done because there were no further demands, requests for this thing to us. But we were not the -- so to say, the organisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: -- to practically organise this transport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And then you said, if I have taken correct notes, that the team should go to the hospital to check the bodies, whether they were mutilated. I take it that was another statement made by Croatian representatives.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I would say that the Bosnian Croat representatives, HDZ in Zenica, they requested us to go to the hospital to, if I say so, control the corpses. And the reason for that was that often in these type of situations rumours very fast increased and were spread that the corpses were -- or the persons were mutilated, tortured, whatever, before they were killed. And most probably HDZ wanted to have that confirmed. We wanted to ourselves have an, exact, objective understanding, so we could either -- so we could say it was or say they were not mutilated, and because of that we could maybe try to calm down the tension, which otherwise should go very high very fast. So that's -- it was an interest, both from HDZ and from us ourselves, but of different reasons, to check the bodies or the corpses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But you yourself never visited the place.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: -- the day after, other activities came and we got other orders which had higher priority than this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: You also said us that you left on the 1st of February and that you returned after a while back to Zenica. You also said before the break about the joint commission that the matter was discussed there of the death of the 14 Croats. You said something like the following: "I remember well we found that this matter was not of the highest priority," and that was also the opinion of the HVO representative in the commission. Was that before you left to Split or was it afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That was before I left for Split. It was, if I remember correctly, the first meeting after the joint commission was organised, when we had both parties, and we checked what the situation was in -- or in totally and also different hot spots and so on. And this subject was raised, but there were no demands from the HVO representative, Mr. Nakic, to continue with this examination of the corpses. There were other things which we together found more important to deal with. So we felt in the ECMM part of the commission we shouldn't use the time for the thing, because it was not as important as other more, if I say so, more complicated or difficult questions at that time. The events came very fast, so we had to change our planning from day to day, what to do, what to concentrate on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And apparently this was also your opinion, I think.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few minor clarifications to ask of you, though really I would need several hours to ask all the questions that I would wish. But as our time is limited, I will limit my questions too. You said a moment ago that you met the commander of the 3rd Corps, in answering a question from Judge Swart. Could you tell us at what time this meeting took place with the commander of the 3rd Corps. Was it in the morning, the afternoon, at midday? Roughly about what time?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Well, I'm just sitting now trying to figure out which exact date, which exact hour. Well, I believe, but I do not know exactly, it was afternoon, maybe in the afternoon, early in the afternoon, but I'm sorry to say I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you met the commander, you were not speaking the B/C/S language. You must have had an interpreter with you.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Yes. The system was that we always had one of our four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not asking you the system. Was an interpreter with you during the meeting that you had with the commander of the 3rd Corps? Was there an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember the name of the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you referred to the fact that there were 14 dead, 14 killed - after all, this is a significant number - in the political, military, strategic analysis, did you ask yourself whether this event, when 14 people were killed, did it fit into a more broader context and did you endeavour to find out what actually happened on the 26th of January in that part of the country? Because you were a monitor; therefore, a monitor is there to monitor, to observe. What was your conclusion as to what had happened on the 26th of January?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: My conclusion was that something had happened, either a fight between HVO people and 3rd Corps people. When I say "people," I mean soldiers. Or it was some form of attack from soldiers from 3rd Corps against these three villages, which I didn't know at that time exactly where, to try to get control of that part of the terrain. But I also said to myself or we two in the team discussed and found out it was most important to try to solve the problem with these refugees in Zenica first and then try to find out the situation on the spot. And because of that, I think I had a meeting -- you asked earlier -- with Mr. Hadzihasanovic in the afternoon. Time was running fast in the afternoon, and it was not too positive to go in the terrain when it was dark because of security reasons, so we didn't have too much time that day to do everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said in answering a question from the Defence or the Prosecution - I'm not sure - that you heard on that day shells that were falling somewhere. According to your recollection, were these shells coming from 122-millimetre mortars or from a gun? You're a specialist, because you were in an armoured regiment. The number of shells, judging by the sound, were coming from how far from Zenica? And what did this mean to you, in military terms?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I remember that these shells, approximately 20 explosions came at approximately 11.00 and maybe five minutes -- a period of five minutes. The sounds came from south of Zenica, and we were in the centre or in Zenica. And the direction, south of Zenica, that was the direction of Busovaca. That was what we could conclude. If it was 12.2-centimetre Howitzer shooting or some other things, couldn't be clarified. But I can just say that with my experience from tanks, it was no tank shelling, because it's another sound. Most probably it was artillery or maybe mortars. And we could just find out the place, so to say, by sound for the hitting ground. We couldn't hear any sound of -- from where these shells were fired. It was too far away, I presume. So we couldn't find out from which area these shells were fired. And the distance from our place in Zenica to the area where the shells exploded were very difficult to say, but they were some kilometres. So it was difficult to more exactly find out the details concerning this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I'm looking at the time, and to my great regret I will stop with my questions. I turn now to the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, yesterday, when we were discussing this event, I drew your attention to the fact that in two of your statements, the statement you gave in 1997 and the second one in 2001, there are certain differences with respect to this event. At the time we looked at those statements together and we saw that in your statement of 1997 you just said that on the 27th of January there was shelling of the south-east of Zenica from the direction of Busovaca. "I heard at least 20 explosions. They called us from Zenica HVO and asked for assistance. We went to meet with the leader of the HDZ in Zenica. They informed us there that several men had been killed, Bosnian Croats in villages east of Busovaca." And in your statement of 2001, you spoke at what greater detail, so I'll leave out the part referring to the shelling. I shall just read a few excerpts from that statement: At the HDZ in Zenica, you learnt that on the previous day 14 Croats had been captured and then killed in three villages east of Busovaca. No names of villages were mentioned. "The relatives of the Croats were brought to Zenica by bus and they stayed in relatives' and friends' houses in Zenica. I remember wondering why the relatives had come to Zenica, a town dominated by Muslims, whereas Busovaca was much closer and the dominant population were Croats." And then you go on to say that they asked you for transportation assistance and then you said: "In a meeting with Hadzihasanovic at 14.30 that day, we didn't go to the hospital to see the bodies. We informed Hadzihasanovic about the killing of Croatian villagers that we had learnt about from representatives of the HDZ." Is it true that you checked through your personal notes and that you established that the more correct version was the one you gave in 2001, because in your notes you had noted that the HDZ had informed you that these Croats had been captured and then killed; that is, 14 persons, which you hadn't said before, and that also you had a note about your meeting with Commander Hadzihasanovic? Did you do that yesterday during our conversation?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: Did I do what yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Check these facts in your own personal notes and found that in fact what you said in your statement of 2001 corresponded to what you had noted down in your personal notes.

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I did that check, and what is stated 2001 is according to my notes. The reason may be for what I said or what was written down in the statement from 1997 is that in general that statement is shorter, fewer details, because it was the first interrogation and it was a lot said concerning different things in Bosnia and not every detail was written down by the people doing these interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Colonel, that you also checked to see what you said to Commander Hadzihasanovic during that conversation and that your note said that you asked him to assist in the transport of refugees and in the burial of these dead bodies? Is that what you found in your notes?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I found in my notes that I said that I wanted to have the assistance or help, or cooperation, from Mr. Hadzihasanovic or 3rd Corps concerning the transport of refugees and assuring that these bodies should be decently buried, yes. That's my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you also confirm that in answer to my question as to whether you spoke to the Commander Hadzihasanovic at the time about killing, crimes and other matters that you were told about in the HDZ, your answer was that you didn't discuss this with Commander Hadzihasanovic but that you only requested his assistance for the transportation of the relatives and the burial of the bodies. Was that the answer that you gave me?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: I informed Mr. Hadzihasanovic of this request and this information, true or not true, from HDZ people. I didn't in these discussions with Mr. Hadzihasanovic discuss if it should be a crime of war. I did not do that. And rather fast we came to that part of this discussion concerning how to solve this practical problem with the refugees and concentrated on that matter, where in that matter Mr. Hadzihasanovic gave a positive attitude to solve the problem practically. But I didn't discuss if it was a crime of war or not. That was not in this situation any reason to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, when you checked through your notes, you didn't find any note saying that you informed Hadzihasanovic about the killing of these people, that is, that you had informed him that those persons had been captured and then killed. This is a fact that is not to be found in your notes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In my notes I written the information I got from the HDZ people, is that these 14 Bosnian Croats had been captured and then killed. That was what the HDZ people told me. I am not controlled it myself. I had no chance to do that. But I was told they were captured and then killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally don't know whether there were 14 people; you don't know whether they were killed; you don't know where that event took place nor how it took place, because you did not have a chance to verify any of those facts. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MATS TORPING
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have the other attorneys any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no additional questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Colonel, we wish to thank you for coming to testify in The Hague. You have answered questions put to you by the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, and the Judges. We thank you for your contribution to the establishment of the truth, and we wish you a safe journey home. I'm going to ask the usher to be kind enough to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I shall give you the floor for your to tell us about tomorrow's hearing. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The witness who's on the letter that was previously provided to the Trial Chamber and the Defence will be here tomorrow for purposes of cross-examination by the Defence and, of course, to answer any questions from Your Honours on perhaps any issues arising from that cross-examination or examination by the Bench he will be available for

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave and with the assistance of all of the hard-working people who assist us in and around the courtroom, if I could just address Your Honours on an issue for just a couple of moments. I was informed yesterday by the Chamber's legal officer to be prepared to put onto the record information concerning a meeting that was held between the Chamber's legal officer and the senior trial attorney, Mr. Withopf, concerning the Trial Chamber's oral order of 17 May 2004. I am prepared to do that perhaps tomorrow, time permitting. Alternatively, I can reduce that information to writing and file that, if that would be of greater assistance. There is one issue, however, that I wanted to alert Your Honours about as quickly as possible; that concerns some of the additional witnesses that we have been ordered by Your Honours to produce in order to testify. My colleague, Ms. Benjamin, next week will be in Bosnia interviewing these individuals. It is unlikely, Mr. President, that all of these individuals will be available for testifying in the following week, that is, the week of 7 June. And I'm simply seeking some guidance from the Trial Chamber - perhaps we could get that tomorrow prior to Ms. Benjamin's departure - as to whether or not the Chamber would prefer to have those witnesses in effect made available as they are available or if we might be in the unfortunate situation of having to have a brief adjournment, perhaps for a week or even longer, and then bring all of those witnesses so that they can testify consecutively, rather than perhaps one on the 7th and one on the 10th and one on the 14th. I hope you see the point I'm trying to make, Mr. President. I don't want to be in a position where we have only one or two witnesses per week for the next couple of weeks. And I simply raise that issue so that perhaps we could have some guidance so that when Ms. Benjamin meets with these witnesses they can be properly informed as to when they might be here and she can then give them clearer information as to the way that the Trial Chamber wishes to proceed. I thank Your Honours for the opportunity to bring this up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding this point, the Judges have discussed it amongst themselves. Of course, it is up to the Prosecution to see at what appropriate time it would call these witnesses, to have absolutely freedom of manoeuvre regarding the dates when you wish to have these witnesses testify. If you feel that they should also appear at the same time - a priori it seems like a good idea - the only question that the Chamber is concerned about is to make sure that the Prosecution case should close sometime in June, and of course one shouldn't have holes in the timetable of witnesses. What you could perhaps do, together with the Defence, to have a provisional chart filling in the boxes for the weeks to come, and then you will let us know and we will say, "Yes, there's no problem there." But I know that you have a lot of problems, scheduling problems, whether the witnesses will be available or not. These are real problems. And it's a good idea to send a Prosecutor to interview those people on the spot, to see how and when they are available. So we will talk about it again, but I am telling you in very general terms what our views are. Has the Defence any observations to make in this connection, though these are Prosecution witnesses? But any observation is always welcome. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, of course the Prosecution must propose how they intend to complete their case. It is up to them and they're quite aware of that. The problem that my learned friend has mentioned does affect the work of the Defence as well, however, so if possible we would like to agree on hearing the witnesses in continuity, rather than having breaks of one day in between. If we need to have a break, we believe it would be better to have a break of several days, which would give the Defence an opportunity to devote its attention to the preparations of its own case and to be able to plan accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no observations those matter. It's really a question of when the witnesses are going to be available. And that's something that is difficult to speculate about now. We'll know once the investigations are complete, which witnesses and when, and then it will be clearer what the schedule could be. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In any event, the parties should continue their dialogue, and one of the solutions would be to have a provisional table to allow both parties to have a clearer idea. But we will deal with it when you let us know. I apologise again to the interpreters. We have overstepped the time once again. I thank everyone for their contribution, and I invite you to come back for the hearing tomorrow, which will start at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.58 p.m.,
